1 Executive Summary

1.1. Product Introduction

Merck, Sharp, & Dohme, Corp. is seeking the approval of a New Molecular Entity (NME). This
NME is a monoclonal antibody directed at Toxin B of Clostridium difficile and has been
designated as MK-6072. The applicant is seeking the indication of prevention of Clostridium
difficile Infection (CDI) recurrence in patients 18 years or older receiving antibiotic therapy for
CDI.

1.2. Conclusions on the Substantial Evidence of Effectiveness

This reviewer recommends that MK-6072 be approved for the prevention of recurrence of CDI
in subjects 18 years and older. The drug’s effect on preventing recurrence appears variably
persuasive, both statistically and clinically, in studies PO0O1 and P002. Though, a potentially
harmful effect of MK-6072 on initial clinical cure cannot be ruled out given the inconsistent
findings in study P001 and P002, further analysis appears to diminish the clinical significance of
several of those deemed failures of initial treatment. Still, the potential negative findings relative
to clinical cure should be made clear in labelling, and clinicians should use clinical judgment in
deciding the best candidates for this therapy.

2 Therapeutic Context

2.1. Analysis of Condition

Clostridium difficile infection is a well-recognized cause of colitis associated with morbidity and
mortality, particularly in hospitalized patients and patients in long-term care facilities. It is
implicated in 20-30% of patients with antibiotic-associated diarrhea, and 50-75% of those with
antibiotic-associated colitis. It is a gram positive, spore forming, anaerobic rod-shaped bacterium
which colonizes subjects through the fecal-oral route. Toxin-producing C. difficile may expand
and cause infection in the colon, particularly in those persons with recent disruptions to their
colonic flora by antimicrobial or chemotherapeutic exposure. It mediates its disease activity
through toxin production, particularly through toxins A and B (though other unknown
mechanisms of action/toxin actions are likely at play as well). These toxins are thought to have
harmful effects on the colonic epithelium and induce deleterious secretory, inflammatory, and
apoptotic processes. The toxins appear to disrupt cytoskeletal regulation eventually resulting in
cell rounding in death. Toxin A mediates fluid secretion and an inflammatory response. Toxin
B’s mechanism of action is less well-understood but appears to be more potent that Toxin A.
CDI can be distinguished by strain, particularly by ribotyping of the spacer region 16S and 23S
1DNA. Notably, particular strains such as NAP 1/027 have been associated with epidemic
disease.

Subjects suffering from infection may range from having mild diarrhea, to significant colitis
leading to colectomy and, possibly, death. Symptoms are often associated with fever and
leukocytosis. Occasionally, subjects may not have diarrhea but may instead present with a toxic
megacolon, a potentially life threatening complication. Diagnosis of the disease is most often
made with a combination of clinical suspicion (due to diarrhea in a hospitalized elderly patient,
etc.) and a positive ELISA for Toxin A or B or both. These ELISA tests have variable sensitivity
but are commonly used due to their ease of testing and cheap expense. Increasingly, PCR-based
tests that assess for the toxin-producing genes are also being used.

The initial infection episode is often successfully managed by fluid replacement, discontinuation
of the offending agent such as an antimicrobial (if possible), and oral/IV antimicrobial therapy
with oral metronidazole, vancomycin, or fidaxomicin (and occasionally IV metronidazole or
rectally delivered vancomycin or metronidazole). Second —line agents used very infrequently
include nitazoxanide and rifamycin as well as cytotoxin binding agents such as cholestyramine
or colestipol. However, a significant proportion (estimates are wide-ranging from a quarter to
almost half of patients) of treated subjects will experience a recurrence of CDI, including elderly
subjects, subjects with previous episodes of diarrhea or underlying morbidity, and subjects
infected with particular strains. There are no approved therapies for the treatment of recurrences.

2.2. Analysis of Current Treatment Options

Though treatment of an initial episode of CDI is relatively straightforward, generally involving
10-14 day courses of oral vancomycin, oral fidaxomicin, or oral metronidazole (sometimes
combined with intravenous metronidazole in severe cases), there is no approved or well-studied
definitive treatment for prevention of recurrences. As to the treatment of recurrent episodes of
CDI, a repeat of the initial regimen is commonly given and is often successful for the first
recurrence. In cases of repeat recurrences, prolonged/tapering oral vancomycin regimens, pulsed
oral vancomycin therapy, administration of immunoglobulins (particularly in cases of
hypogammglobulinemia), probiotic administration and fecal transplant have all been advocated.
While fecal transplant also shows promise for prevention of recurrences, this therapy has not
been rigorously studied or received regulatory approval. Also, its production has yet to be
streamlined.

3 Regulatory Background

3.1. U.S. Regulatory Actions and Marketing History
MK-6072 is an NME that has not been approved or marketed anywhere in the world.
3.2. Summary of Presubmission/Submission Regulatory Activity

The initial investigational new drug application (IND) for human monoclonal antibodies against
C. difficile toxin A and toxin B was submitted on November 25, 2005. Early in product
development, the applicant hypothesized that an anti-toxin A antibody or the combination of
anti-toxin A and B antibodies would be the most effective in prevention of CDI recurrence.

The first Phase 2 trial evaluated the efficacy and safety of a single infusion of an anti-toxin A
antibody versus placebo. The trial was conducted in 2005-2006 and was terminated early after
enrolling 46 subjects because emerging non-clinical data suggested that the combination of
antibodies against toxin A and B would be more effective for the prevention of CDI recurrence.

A Phase 2 study comparing a combination of C. difficile toxin A and B antibodies with placebo
in patients receiving antibacterial therapy for CDI was conducted in 2006-2008. The study
enrolled 101 patients in the combination arm and 99 patients in the placebo arm. The recurrence
tate was lower among patients treated with the combination therapy (7% vs. 25%; p < 0.001). No
Phase 2 studies evaluated bezlotoxumab alone.

Subsequently, the applicant proposed to conduct Phase 3 studies comparing the combination of
monoclonal antibodies to C. difficile toxins A and B with placebo. On May 12, 2010 the

FDA, in keeping with the “combination rule” outlined in CFR 300.50(a), recommended studying

antibodies to C. difficile toxins A and B, antibody to C. difficile toxin A alone, antibody to C. 
difficile toxin B alone, and placebo, all given in conjunction with standard of care antimicrobial 
therapy for CDI.

On December 21, 2010 a Special Protocol Assessment (SPA) agreement was reached on the 
design of study P001, a Phase 3, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, adaptive-design 
study of the efficacy in the prevention of CDI recurrence of a single infusion of human 
monoclonal antibody to C. difficile toxin A, human monoclonal antibody to C. difficile toxin B, 
and the combination of human monoclonal antibodies to C. difficile toxin A and toxin B in 
patients receiving antibacterial therapy for C. difficile infection. The primary endpoint in the 
protocol was CDI recurrence following clinical cure of baseline CDI episode.  The proportion 
was calculated as the number of subjects with CDI recurrence divided by the total number of 
subjects in the analysis population regardless of whether or not they had a successful resolution 
of the initial episode of CDI. 

However, upon review of Protocol P002 FDA recommended changing the primary endpoint 
from CDI recurrence to global cure. The reason for the recommendation was the concern that in 
the calculation of the CDI recurrence rate, subjects who failed treatment of the initial CDI 
episode would be counted as not having a recurrence.  For this binary endpoint, a successful 
outcome would group those who were initially cured and did not have a recurrence with those 
who failed initial treatment. Subsequently a greater number of initial cure failures in a treatment 
group would result in a smaller number of subjects who could potentially develop recurrence. 
Therefore, an imbalance between treatment groups in the number of subjects who failed 
treatment of the initial CDI episode could confound the assessment of recurrence rates.  This 
would be most concerning if the monoclonal antibody arm had a lower initial cure rate than 
placebo.  The endpoint of global cure rate avoids this problem by defining treatment success as 
clinical cure of the initial CDI episode AND the absence of CDI recurrence. In August 2012 
FDA conveyed their recommendations to the applicant. 

The applicant disagreed with changing the primary endpoint. Global Cure remained a key 
secondary endpoint in both trials. FDA acknowledged that the Phase 3 trials would preserve the 
use of CDI recurrence rate as the primary efficacy analysis but noted that interpretation of the 
results of these trials would depend on the number of subjects with clinical cure of the initial 
infection. 

In November 2015 the applicant submitted a BLA with the results of two Phase 3 pivotal trials to 
support approval of bezlotoxumab for the prevention of C. difficile infection recurrence.

4.4. Nonclinical Pharmacology/Toxicology

Single and repeat intermittent-dose toxicology studies in mice with IV bezlotoxumab
administered for 14 days (5 doses/3 day interval) and 21 days (2 doses/14 day interval) were
conducted. These failed to demonstrate any clinical signs or evidence of toxicity, at doses up to
50 and 125 mg/kg respectively, and at approximately 2.5 and 7 times greater exposure than
observed in the clinic after a single 10 mg/kg dose. All histopathological evaluations of tissues
from bezlotoxumab treated animals were similar to controls. No targets of bezlotoxumab toxicity
were identified in any of the animal toxicology studies. Tissue cross-reactivity studies were
conducted in vitro in at least 38 mouse and human tissues with bezlotoxumab. They showed no
reactivity (positive staining) of tissue samples. No genotoxicity, reproductive/developmental
toxicity, or carcinogenicity studies were conducted with bezlotoxumab.

45. Clinical Pharmacology

4.5.1. Mechanism of Action

MK-6072 binds to toxin B secreted by toxin producing C. difficile during acute infection.
Theoretically, such binding might limit further epithelial and inflammatory damage incited by
the toxin, however exactly how binding of the toxin during initial infection prevents recurrence
is unclear.

4.5.2. Pharmacodynamics

As bezlotoxumab is a monoclonal antibody to an exogenous toxin, it has no intrinsic
antimicrobial activity. It binds toxin B with an affinity equilibrium dissociation constant (Kd) of
<1 x 10-9 M. In Vero cells 200 mcg/mL of bezlotoxumab could block binding of 50 ng/mL toxin
B. Simuiarly, in Caco-2 cells the addition of bezlotoxumab (in concentraions 0-100mcg/ml)
resulted in a dose-dependent neutralizing effect of 100ng/ml of toxin B as measured by
transepithelial resistance.

4.5.3. Pharmacokinetics

Bezlotoxumab has a half-life of roughly 19 days and volume of distribution of 7.33L. It has
characteristics typical of other monoclonal antibodies including limited extravascular distribution
and tissue binding, and minimal renal clearance. It is degraded into small proteins and amino

The Clinical Review of this application was divided between two different reviewers. Dr.

Efficacy

The review of clinical efficacy was primarily focused on the two pivotal Phase 3 studies —
studies P0O1 and P002. Because the sponsor ultimately chose to pursue MK-6072 for this
indication, earlier Phase 2 trials were less useful in evaluating efficacy because either they did
not have a MK-6072 alone arm or did not evaluate MK-6072 at all. Similarly, in evaluation of
the Phase 3 trials, almost all of the focus in this review has been on the comparison of MK-6072
with placebo. The MK-3415 (human monoclonal antibodies to C. difficile toxin A) and MK-
3415A (human monoclonal antibodies to C. difficile toxin A and toxin B) arms are discussed
sparsely.

For the purposes of clinical efficacy, the sponsor’s results were evaluated and interpreted in
detail by both the statistical reviewer, Dr. Cheryl Dixon, and by Dr. Mishra. Because there was
concern over the use of the primary endpoint of recurrence and how recurrence was defined (see
below), numerous sensitivity analyses were performed by both the clinical and statistics
reviewers using SAS, JMP, JReview, etc. in order to more fully inform the reported results.
Both the statistical and clinical reviewer attempted to redefine recurrence more robustly and thus
their respective major findings may differ to a degree from the sponsor as well as from each

Overview and Objective

P001: The purpose of the MODIFY I trial was to determine whether the infusion of the 
combined monoclonal antibodies to C. difficile toxins A and B (MK-3415A) in conjunction with 
standard of care was superior to the infusion of monoclonal antibody to toxin A only (MK-3415) 
plus standard of care , the infusion of monoclonal antibody to toxin B only (MK-6072) plus 
standard of care , and placebo plus standard of care in preventing the recurrence of C. difficile 
infection over a period of 12 weeks.  The trial was also designed to potentially show the 
superiority of MK-3415 plus standard of care or MK-6072 plus standard of care over placebo 
plus standard of care in preventing recurrence.

P002: Similar to that of P001 except that there was no antitoxin A alone arm (MK-3415).

Trial Design

 P001

This was a randomized, double-blind, placebo controlled, multicenter, adaptive design study 
evaluating the recurrence of C. difficile infection (CDI) in subjects receiving a single intravenous 
infusion of  monoclonal antibodies to both toxin A and toxin B, individual monoclonal 
antibodies to toxin A or toxin B alone, or placebo along with standard of care antimicrobial 
therapy . The study was designed to evaluate recurrence over a 12 week period post infusion. 
The trial involved 184 sites worldwide including sites in North and South America, Europe, 
Africa, and Australia; there were 75 sites in the United States. 1600 subjects were planned for 
enrollment.

Appropriately, the study was placebo controlled/blinded as there is no currently approved drug to 
prevent recurrence of C. difficile infection (CDI).  The study was also designed to meet the 
combination rule (in this case demonstrating the superiority of the combination antibody arm 
over the individual antibody arms in preventing recurrence).  The follow up time of 12 weeks 
would be expected to capture a significant portion of recurrences though CDI recurrences have 
been known to occur after even longer intervals.  All subjects received standard of care 
antimicrobial therapy, which appropriately mimicked the likely adjunct use of the study drug that 
would occur in a clinical setting.  

A subject could be included in the trial if he/she had CDI as defined by 3 or more loose stools in 
the prior 24 hours and a positive stool test for toxigenic C. difficile in the seven days prior to 
infusion. This is similar to the diagnostic criteria used in the recent approval for fidaxomicin, 
although in those studies the toxin test had to have been positive in the previous 48 hours.

The inclusion and exclusion criteria were appropriately narrow.  Elderly subjects and subjects 
with significant illness (such as renal or hepatic dysfunction) were not necessarily excluded 
however there were some exclusions based on the use of concomitant medications that might

Study Endpoints 

P001: 

The primary endpoint for this study is the proportion of subjects in each arm [using the full 
analysis set (FAS) population set defined below] that have a recurrence of CDI through week 12 
following clinical cure of the initial episode.  Recurrence is defined as 3 or more watery stools in 
24 hours associated with a positive local or central lab test for toxigenic C difficile.

Secondary endpoints include recurrence in particular clinically relevant subgroups as well as the 
proportion of subjects in each arm with a Global Cure – i.e.  cure of the initial CDI episode and 
no recurrence through week 12. 

Exploratory endpoints include time to CDI recurrence and proportion of subjects with initial 
clinical cure. Initial clinical cure is defined as the proportion of subjects in each arm who have 
taken ≤ 14 days of SOC and have ≤ 2 loose stools in 24 hours for 2 consecutive days after 
completing SOC.  Other exploratory endpoints included time to initial clinical cure, proportion 
of subjects with diarrhea recurrence (regardless of  whether there is an associated positive toxin 
test for C. difficile), and the proportion of subjects who had WBC ≤ 10,000 on Days 4 and 11 and 
temperature < 101.0° F by Day 4 and 11]

It is important to note that from the Agency perspective, recurrence was not considered the only 
relevant endpoint for both the P001 and P002 trials; cure of the initial episode was considered 
just as important especially as many subjects were getting the study drug early on in their SOC 
course.  The sponsor’s focus on recurrence as the primary endpoint does not account for potential 
trial outcomes in which a drug causes a decrease in initial cures while providing protection 
against recurrence in those subjects who are initial cures.

Durability of Response

As has already been discussed, both studies P001 and P002 assessed for recurrences over a

nine months (the extension cohort). 293 of these subjects were a part of the FAS (112 subjects in

global cures over the 12 month period in the extension cohort, the MK-6072 arm did
considerably better than placebo (69.7% global cures vs. 40.2%, respectively). However, the
extension cohort appeared to differ significantly from the full P0O2 FAS. In fact the rate of
recurrence over the 12 week study period in the full FAS set in the placebo arm was 25.7% while
it was 41.5% over the same period for the placebo arm of the extension cohort (using the sponsor
definition for recurrence). Thus, it is difficult to draw any real conclusions regarding durability

Secondly, it is important to consider how clinicians might use any therapy directed toward 
preventing recurrence.  In an ideal scenario, any adjunct therapy to prevent recurrence would be 
given at the time of/right after initial clinical cure.  This would spare the clinician and patient the 
risk and cost associated with administering the adjunct therapy early in the course of the initial 
CDAD episode.  Such risk would include administering adjunct therapy to a subject that was 
never cured initially (in which case preventing recurrence becomes moot) or administering 
therapy that might somehow actually interfere with the SOC treatment of the initial episode.  

Bearing the above considerations in mind, one can now evaluate the data submitted in this 
application.

In regards to recurrences, no matter what definitions of recurrence or clinical cure was used (the 
original applicant definitions of recurrence  and cure, the reviewer expanded definition of 
recurrence, or the applicant expanded definition of clinical cure), bezlotoxumab appeared to 
either have a statistically significant effect or a trend toward lessening recurrences. 

Using the reviewer expanded definition of recurrence that captures subjects not tested for toxin 
upon recurrence of diarrhea as well as those who used therapies that could essentially treat CDI, 
MK-6072 appears to perform well relative to placebo in P001 and marginally better in study 
P002. In P001, MK-6072 had an absolute reduction in recurrence rate of 13.6%. Moreover, MK-
6072 appeared to do better than placebo in preventing recurrence in almost all subgroups tested.  
In study P002, MK-6072 had absolute reduction in recurrence rate of 5.3%. Though this 
reduction was modest, the MK-6072 arm had lower recurrence rates in almost every subgroup 
(except, importantly, in males). 

It is interesting to note that in P001 administration of SOC for ≤ 3 days before study drug 
infusion was associated with “less” favorable outcomes, and in P002, administration of SOC for 
5-6 days before study drug infusion was associated with “more” favorable outcomes.  Whether 
this is reflective of an overall improved activity of MK-6072 on recurrence when given later in 
the initial course of SOC is unclear, particularly given that the opposite effect was seen in 
subjects who had received >6 days of SOC before receiving study drug infusion (though the 
sample  size in this subgroup is quite small).  It should be noted that the original recurrence 
definition did not distinguish between those requiring treatment and those who did not.  
However, there appeared to be a trend toward less need for treatment in the bezlotoxumab arm; 
this was in conjunction with other exploratory analyses that seemed to suggest some decreased 
severity of recurrence with bezlotoxumab. Overall, there appears to be a modest to moderate 
effect of MK-6072 on recurrence.

study P001 with an absolute reduction in clinical cure of 5.3%. MK-6072 also performed worse 
in virtually every subgroup analyzed in this study. In study P002, MK-6072 had the opposite

several subgroups where placebo performed numerically better than MK-6072. In terms of the 
duration of SOC prior to receiving study drug infusion, no clear trend can be seen from the two 
trials (although in subjects >6 days of SOC there was trend toward better clinical cures in the 
MK-6072 arm; again, the sample size was quite small).  Thus, MK-6072’s effect on initial 
clinical cure is unclear. However, in exploratory analyses using the expanded definition of 
clinical cure, the rates of clinical cure in study arms are similar and it appears that many of 
clinical failures defined according to the original cure definition were only modestly clinically 
significant. A subset review of CRFs of reclassified cures from P001 did not provide any clear 
link between administration of bezlotoxumab and initial clinical failure.  In totality, 
bezlotoxumab may have a negative effect on clinical cure, but it appears to be clinically minor 
and such risk may be tolerable in high benefit scenarios. 

Overall, when looking at the effect of MK-6072 on the two most important clinical parameters, 
recurrence and initial clinical cure, a positive risk benefit calculus seems plausible.  There is 
certainly a level of uncertainty when relying on stool diaries, etc. but hopefully in this blinded 
trial those uncertainties are minimized. . In general, there appears to be a moderate reduction in 
recurrences at the possible expense of small increases in mostly minor initial clinical failures. 
Still, this would place the significant risk-benefit calculus involved in deciding whether or not to 
prescribe the study drug to a patient with CDI at the feet of clinicians, when ideally this process 
should have been definitively made much earlier- i.e.-during this drug development and 
regulatory review process. 

It is imperative that clinicians use the drug judiciously, hopefully reserving its use for those 
subjects with significant risk factors for recurrence.  Given the likely cost of this medication, 
such decision-making is even more imperative.  Ideally, proper guidance regarding the timing of 
study drug relative to SOC would have been delineated from the trial results but given the 
heterogeneous nature of drug receipt relative to SOC as well as the heterogeneous results, no 
clear recommendation can be made with regard to timing of bezlotoxumab.
The Division and Applicant may consider a PMR/PMC for a study evaluating the timing of study 
drug administration relative to SOC in regards to effects on both clinical cure and recurrence.  
Such a study should have a mutually agreed upon definition of clinical cure and recurrence and 
could stratify subjects based on timing of SOC.

8 Review of Safety

8.1. Safety Review Approach

This safety review focuses on data from the safety population enrolled in the two Phase 3
randomized, placebo-controlled trials, study P00O1 and P002, supporting this application. These
two studies evaluated the efficacy, safety and tolerability of a single infusion of bezlotoxumab
(bezlo) alone and in combination with actoxumab (acto) for prevention of Clostridium difficile
infection (CDI) in patients receiving standard of care antibacterial therapy (oral vancomycin,
fidaxomicin, oral or intravenous metronidazole). Both bezlo and acto are fully human
monoclonal antibodies: bezlo is an anti- type B Clostridium difficile toxin antibody and acto is an
anti-type A Clostridium difficile toxin antibody.

The two studies are similar in design with the following exceptions: the first study, study P001,
followed an adaptive design. It also had four arms study arms: subjects that received acto
infusion only (acto arm), subjects that received bezlo infusion alone (bezlo arm), subjects that
received combination of acto and bezlo infusions (acto+bezlo arm), and subjects that received
normal saline infusion (placebo arm). In addition, study P001 had a planned interim analysis at
40% enrollment to evaluate each study arm and to drop one of the single therapy arms if it did
not demonstrate efficacy more than the combination arm. Based on the interim analysis, which
showed worsening outcome in the acto arm as compared to all three arms, the acto arm was
dropped for the post-interim analysis study period. Study P002 did not have planned interim
analysis and was designed with only 3 arms: bezlo arm, acto+bezlo arm and placebo arm. In
addition, study P002 had an extended safety cohort of 300 participants that were followed for
additional 9 months after the 12-week study period. Given the similarity in study design,
including adverse event (AE) reporting period, pooled data from study P001 and P002 are
presented.

The safety population included subjects in Study P001 and P002 that received partial or full
infusion of bezlo, acto+bezlo or placebo. Of note, subjects that received acto alone were
excluded from the safety population. However, data from the acto arm is presented separately for
completeness of the review since the safety population includes subjects that received the
combined acto+bezlo infusion. Also, data from a phase 2 study that compared the combination of
acto and bezlo with placebo, study P017, is not pooled with the phase 3 studies mentioned above
due to difference in AE reporting time frame The safety data for this study is presented
separately.

Since bezlo is a monoclonal antibody, special attention was given to adverse events related to
immunogenicity, and infusion-related adverse reactions.

8.9. Safety in the Postmarket Setting

8.9.1. Safety Concerns Identified Through Postmarket Experience

The study drug is a novel biologic, and thus, there is no postmarket experience.

8.9.2. Expectations on Safety in the Postmarket Setting

Since the mechanism of action for this monoclonal antibody is not fully elucidated, it is difficult
to anticipate all the potential off-target effects. Hence, postmarketing pharmacovigilance is
recommended.

In addition, there are only 29 subjects that received more than one dose of bezlo in a Phase 1
study of healthy volunteers. Hence, there is minimal data as to the safety of repeated doses of
bezlo. In the post-marketing setting, it is possible that patients may receive more than one dose
of bezlo, especially patients who attend multiple health care facilities.

As mentioned earlier, there is paucity of minorities in the Phase 3 trials. Although the subgroup

analysis based on ethnicity did not show major differences in AE rates or mortality, the small
numbers may not allow for detection of some safety signals in subpopulation of minority groups.

8.11. Integrated Assessment of Safety

Summary

Bezlotoxumab, given as a single IV infusion, had an overall favorable safety profile with the
rates of treatment emergent adverse events (TEAE), serious adverse events (SAE) and deaths
similar to placebo. No increase in adverse events (AEs) related to potential immune-mediated
reactions was observed in the bezlotoxumab- treated subjects as compared to placebo- treated
subjects. A safety finding identified during the review of data from the two Phase 3 trials is the
numerically higher numbers of serious adverse events and deaths in bezlotoxumab-treated
subjects with baseline congestive heart failure as compared to placebo.

Discussion

There was adequate number of subjects exposed to bezlo at the proposed dose during the drug
development program. There were 1790 subjects exposed to bezlo either alone or in
combination with acto; 126 were healthy subjects in Phase 1 studies (30 subjects received bezlo
alone and 96 received acto + bezlo), and 1664 were subjects in Phase 2 and 3 (786 received
bezlotoxumab alone and 878 received actot+bezlo). Of these, 1741 subjects were exposed to
bezlo dose at 10mg/kg. With the exception of subjects in study P004 who received two doses of
actot+bezlo (n=30), all subjects were exposed to a single dose of bezlo or actotbezlo.

The safety population is comprised of all subjects in the two Phase 3 studies, studies P0O1 and
P002), that received partial or full infusion of the study medication. For the safety analysis,
subjects were grouped in the treatment arm they received (as treated), as opposed to the group
they were randomized to. Throughout the two pivotal studies, POO1 and P002, there were 212
deaths. Among these, 166 occurred in the safety population because of AEs reported during the
12-week study period. There was no significant difference in the mortality rate of the bezlo
(7.1%) and acto+bezlo (6.6%) arm as compared to placebo (7.1%).

There is no major imbalance in the frequency of serious adverse events among the three arms:
29.4%, 27.3% o and 32.7% of subjects in the bezlo, acto+bezlo and placebo arm, respectively,
experienced at least one SAE in the 12-week study period. In all three arms, the infection,
infestation, and gastrointestinal MedDRA System Organ Classes accounted for the majority of
the SAEs. A detailed look of the SAEs revealed cardiac failure, urinary tract infection, diarrhea,
abdominal pain to have occurred more frequently in the bezlo arm as compared to the placebo
arm. From these, cardiac failure showed the largest risk difference, with 17 subjects (2.2%) in
the bezlo arm as compared to placebo (n=7, 0.009%). Among subjects with baseline diagnosis of
congestive heart failure, more subjects in the bezlo died (23/119 vs. 13/104).

Analysis to evaluate occurrence infusion-related reactions did not reveal a significant difference

changes in systolic pressure over the infusion period, numerically more subjects had either 
decrease in SBP by 30% from baseline or SBP<90mmHg when comparing  the bezlo arm  at 30 
minutes after start of infusion (10 vs. 8) and end of infusion (13 vs. 7).  In total, there were 4 
subjects with potential infusion-related reactions. 

Among the 710 bezlo subjects that had at least one post-infusion anti-drug antibody (ADA) 
testing, none were reported to have developed ADA, although 28% had inconclusive test results. 
The subgroup analysis of adverse events by age, race, sex and body weight did not reveal 
significant differences by the abovementioned variables.  

Overall, one time dose of bezlo appears safe; however, safety, including, immunogenicity, of 
multiple doses of bezlo cannot be assessed based on the data provided.
